title: Latin America’s digital-trade growth is constrained less by online demand than by regional interoperability and capability gaps
source_unit: IDB, World Bank, and WTO, Digital Trade in Latin America and the Caribbean: Connecting Markets, Powering Growth
geography: Latin America and the Caribbean, with regional and subregional digital-trade comparisons and country-level policy analysis

observations.period: 2005-2024; digitally delivered services exports from Latin America and the Caribbean

denominator.unit: Latin America and the Caribbean regional digital-trade economy

export_growth.value: digitally delivered services exports rose nearly fivefold from US$18.5 billion in 2005 to US$87.7 billion in 2024

global_share.value: the region accounted for about 2% of global exports of digitally delivered services in 2024

forward_potential.value: under a scenario combining technological progress with improved policy environments, digitally deliverable services exports could grow by up to 7.9% annually through 2040, with digitalization contributing up to 4.5 percentage points
forward_potential.unit: annual percent growth and percentage points

mechanism.value: rapid digital-export growth coexists with substantial unrealized capability and policy space, so access to digital markets is an infrastructure-and-governance outcome rather than an automatic consequence of connectivity

observations.method: Joint IDB-World Bank-WTO regional report using trade statistics, digital-trade indicators, country comparisons, policy analysis, and scenario modeling.
observations.uncertainty: The 2040 estimate is a scenario rather than a forecast or causal treatment effect; it depends on technology, policy, investment, and country-specific implementation assumptions.
observations.subgroup: Digital-service exporters, small firms, women-led firms, entrepreneurs, workers, consumers, regulators, and countries with different connectivity, skills, and policy readiness.
observations.counterinterpretation: Export growth can remain concentrated among larger or better-connected firms; improved aggregate exports do not establish broad consumer welfare, worker security, or equal regional participation.

observations.period: 2023; intraregional digitally deliverable services and regional e-commerce traffic

denominator.unit: Latin American and Caribbean regional digital-service and e-commerce flows

intraregional_services.value: intraregional digitally deliverable services exports totaled US$7.8 billion and represented 8.4% of the region’s exports in this category

comparison.value: the intraregional share is below the corresponding shares reported for Europe, Asia, and North America

ecommerce_inbound.value: about 60% of foreign visits to LAC e-commerce platforms originated elsewhere in the region, while only 13% of visits by LAC consumers to foreign platforms went to platforms elsewhere in LAC

regional_springboard.value: neighboring markets can serve as a springboard for smaller service providers and women-led firms before they expand to more distant markets

observations.method: Analysis of digitally deliverable service trade, subregional flows, and e-commerce traffic, combined with firm and exporter evidence on regional-market entry.
observations.uncertainty: Trade and web-traffic shares describe flows and destination patterns; they do not by themselves establish why regional integration is low or whether a regional-market springboard produces durable firm growth.
observations.subgroup: Micro, small, and medium-sized firms, women-led firms, online retailers, digital-service providers, regional consumers, and platforms serving cross-border demand.
observations.counterinterpretation: Consumers may prefer extraregional platforms because of price, selection, trust, network effects, or logistics rather than regulatory fragmentation alone; regional traffic is not equivalent to regional value capture.

observations.period: 2024-2026; enabling conditions for cross-border digital trade in LAC

denominator.unit: policy areas identified by the report: infrastructure, regulation, payment interoperability, trade procedures, export promotion, digital capabilities, finance, and measurement

payment_friction.value: cross-border payments remain slow and costly despite wider availability of fast domestic payment systems

trust_and_safety.value: data protection, privacy, cybersecurity, consumer protection, digital identity, and platform-liability rules are part of the enabling environment, with regulatory readiness uneven across countries

capability_constraints.value: firm capabilities, digital skills, export information, and access to finance shape which businesses can participate

interoperability_route.value: digital trade becomes inclusive only when technical infrastructure, rules, payment rails, logistics, skills, finance, and consumer safeguards work across borders

observations.method: Comparative policy and regulatory assessment across digital infrastructure, market openness, data rules, cybersecurity, payments, customs, export promotion, skills, firm capability, and finance.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies enabling conditions and policy priorities rather than estimating a causal contribution for each reform; regulatory presence does not prove enforcement, trust, or consumer protection in practice.
observations.subgroup: Consumers, small exporters, women-led businesses, platform workers and sellers, payment users, regulators, telecom firms, logistics providers, and cross-border service buyers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stronger regulation can improve trust and inclusion but can also increase compliance costs or fragment markets if rules are not interoperable; openness without safeguards can expose consumers and firms to new risks.

IDB bibliographic record, abstract, publication date, DOI, and headline trade figures.
World Bank document API metadata containing the official PDF URL, abstract, authors, report number, and document identifier.

boundary: This record adds a digital-trade-to-regional-integration mechanism linking online commerce to payment, regulation, privacy, cybersecurity, skills, finance, logistics, and consumer-protection infrastructure. It is descriptive and scenario-based evidence, not proof that any one reform causes exports, that digital growth is inclusive, or that regional platforms will capture the value of regional demand.
